title: Youth opportunity and demographic leverage are diverging between growing lower-income regions and ageing richer regions
source_unit: UN DESA Population Division, World Population Highlights 2026: Youth
geography: Global, regional, and country-group youth population estimates and projections, with youth well-being indicators through 2050

observations.period: 2025-2050; global youth population distribution by country income group

denominator.unit: global population aged 15-24 and UN country-income-group projection frame

global_youth_2025.unit: young people aged 15-24 globally in 2025, approximately

llmic_youth_change.unit: percent projected change in youth population in low- and lower-middle-income countries between 2025 and 2050

humic_youth_change.unit: percent projected change in youth population in high- and upper-middle-income countries between 2025 and 2050

llmic_share_2050.unit: percent of the world's youth projected to live in low- and lower-middle-income countries in 2050

llmic_share_2025.unit: percent of the world's youth living in low- and lower-middle-income countries in 2025

observations.method: UN DESA population estimates and projections for persons aged 15-24, grouped by World Bank income classification and interpreted alongside youth well-being priorities.
observations.uncertainty: Youth projections depend on fertility, mortality, migration, classification changes, and data quality. Income-group averages conceal large country, gender, urban-rural, and within-country differences.
observations.subgroup: Young people aged 15-24 in low- and lower-middle-income countries, high- and upper-middle-income countries, and regions with different demographic trajectories.
observations.counterinterpretation: A growing youth population is not automatically a demographic dividend: without education, health, decent work, rights, and voice, population growth can intensify exclusion and fiscal pressure.

observations.period: 2025-2050; age structure and intergenerational capacity in higher-income countries

denominator.unit: high- and upper-middle-income country-group age-structure projection frame

older_to_youth_2025.unit: approximately one person aged 65 or older for each person aged 15-24 in high- and upper-middle-income countries today

older_to_youth_2050.unit: approximately older persons aged 65 or older for each person aged 15-24 projected by 2050 in high- and upper-middle-income countries

observations.method: UN DESA comparison of youth and older-person population projections by country-income group.
observations.uncertainty: Age-band ratios do not measure dependency, health, productivity, care need, or political influence; migration and policy can materially alter country trajectories.
observations.subgroup: Young people, older people, working-age populations, caregivers, education and labour institutions, and public systems in ageing higher-income settings.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower youth share can coexist with strong youth participation and better outcomes; the projection indicates a need for intergenerational solidarity and sustained youth voice, not inevitable generational conflict.

denominator.unit: global youth policy and well-being evidence frame

priority_domains.value: education, decent work, health and well-being, sexual and reproductive health, safe migration pathways, rights, and meaningful participation
priority_domains.unit: priority policy domains identified by the publication

population_foresight.unit: policy approach linking demographic change to youth investment and participation

observations.method: UN DESA synthesis of demographic projections and comparative evidence on youth livelihoods, health, rights, migration, and participation.
observations.uncertainty: The publication identifies policy priorities and mechanisms; it does not estimate a single causal effect of any investment or establish outcomes for every country.
observations.subgroup: Youth-serving public systems, schools, health services, labour markets, migration institutions, civil society, and young people facing unequal access to opportunity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Policy investment should be rights-based and responsive to youth agency; treating young people only as labour supply or demographic instruments can reproduce exclusion.

related_sources.claim: UN DESA ten key messages for the youth publication.
UN DESA publication record and revised June 2026 report metadata.

boundary: This record adds a youth-demography-to-investment, livelihoods, migration, health, rights, and intergenerational-voice route. It is not respondent-level data, does not measure individual youth attitudes or behavior, and does not establish that demographic structure alone causes economic or political outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN DESA report landing page, ten-key-messages PDF, launch page, and publication record were retrieved; youth population distribution, income-group divergence, age-structure ratio, and policy-priority claims were cross-checked against those materials.
